transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in today?

Hello, Dr. Smith. I keep getting stuck redoing the same checks and routines over and over at work, even when I know they’re unnecessary, and it’s starting to derail my projects and my life. It has gotten to a point where these habits feel completely out of my control.
Do you feel a strong urge to perform these checks because you fear something bad will happen if you don’t?

Yes, absolutely. I get these looping thoughts that if I miss a tiny detail, like a bolt size or a minor tolerance, it will cause a catastrophic failure where parts break and people get hurt. Even though I know it's irrational, the fear is so intense that I end up opening and rechecking the same CAD files or emails up to ten times just to make sure I didn't miss anything.
How long have you been performing these checking rituals, and has the frequency or intensity increased over time?

It started about a year ago during a major product rollout when I was also studying for my PE exam. Since then, the intensity has definitely increased; it went from staying just a little late to spending hours rechecking single files past midnight, which has caused me to miss work deadlines and skip my personal activities.
Do these repetitive thoughts or behaviors continue to trouble you even when you try to ignore or suppress them?

Yes, trying to ignore them actually makes the anxiety much worse and the thoughts more persistent. If I try to resist checking a file, the nagging feeling that I've missed a critical detail grows so intense that I can't focus on anything else. I eventually have to give in and do the check just to get some temporary relief from the panic.

No new symptoms suggest an alternative diagnosis, and features do not align with other major psychiatric categories such as mood or psychotic disorders.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with recurrent intrusive thoughts (obsessions) related to catastrophic failure due to minor errors, and repetitive checking behaviors (compulsions) performed to reduce anxiety, which are time-consuming, cause significant functional impairment, and have persisted for over six months. These features are characteristic of obsessive-compulsive disorder.
